drennan.summary: A subcontractor’s definite bid that the general contractor foreseeably and reasonably relied on in submitting its own bid became irrevocable, under § 90, long enough to give the general a reasonable chance to accept after the award; the subcontractor’s unnoticed mistake did not excuse it, and the general recovered the difference between the bid and the replacement cost.

sections.Parties: William A. Drennan, a licensed general contractor, was the plaintiff and respondent; he sought the extra cost of paving after the subcontractor refused to perform at its quoted price. Star Paving Company was the defendant and appellant, maintaining that its bid was a revocable offer withdrawn before acceptance. The Lancaster school district, which awarded Drennan the main contract, was not a party.
sections.Material Facts: On July 28, 1955 Drennan prepared a bid for the Monte Vista school project in Lancaster, due before 8 p.m. As was customary, subcontractors telephoned their quotations on bidding day; his secretary took fifty to seventy-five. Late that afternoon Star’s estimator quoted $7,131.60 for the paving and repeated the figure while Drennan listened on an extension. It was the lowest paving bid; Drennan used it to compute his total of $317,385, named Star as paving subcontractor as the bidding rules required for subcontractors doing at least half a percent of the work, and posted a ten percent bid bond. He won the contract. The next morning, before he had communicated acceptance, Star’s engineer said the bid was a mistake and could not be honored for less than $15,000. Drennan insisted on performance and, after months seeking replacement bids, hired L & H Paving for $10,948.60.
sections.Procedural History: Drennan sued Star for the additional paving cost. The trial court found that Star had made a definite offer to do the specified work for $7,131.60, that Drennan relied on it in computing his bid and naming Star, and that he had no reason to know of the mistake; it awarded $3,817, the difference between the bid and the reasonable replacement cost, plus costs. Star appealed, arguing that no consideration supported an option, that using the bid formed no bilateral contract, and that it withdrew before acceptance; it also pleaded mistake and attacked the damages allegations. The Supreme Court of California, Justice Traynor writing for a unanimous court, affirmed on December 31, 1958.
sections.Issue: Did Drennan’s foreseeable and reasonable reliance on Star’s definite subcontract bid make the offer temporarily irrevocable, even though he had neither paid for an option nor accepted before Star tried to withdraw? Could Star escape because its bid resulted from mistake, and did Drennan adequately show mitigation and damages?
sections.Holding: Yes. Reasonable, foreseeable reliance producing a prejudicial change of position can support an implied subsidiary promise not to revoke an offer, without bargained-for consideration. Under § 90 of the First Restatement, Star’s bid became irrevocable long enough to give Drennan a reasonable opportunity to accept after the general contract was awarded; using the figure was not itself an acceptance, but reliance protected his later chance to accept. Star’s mistake did not defeat recovery because Drennan had no reason to know of it and had already committed himself, and the evidence showed reasonable mitigation. The $3,817 judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Star had not bargained for Drennan’s use of its bid in exchange for a promise to keep it open, and using the bid did not bind Drennan to award Star the subcontract, so there was neither a paid option nor a bilateral contract. Section 90 supplied the answer. Star submitted its bid to win the subcontract and could expect a low bid to be used in Drennan’s computation and help him win the award. Once Drennan committed himself to the owner at a price built on Star’s figure, fairness required protecting a reasonable opportunity to accept. Section 45’s protection of an offeree who begins the performance a unilateral offer invites supplied an analogy: an implied subsidiary promise keeps the offer open, and foreseeable preacceptance reliance justified comparable protection. The protection has limits: a general contractor may not delay acceptance while shopping for a better price or reopen bargaining while holding the bid in reserve,. Mistake did not shift the loss, because Drennan lacked notice of error and paving quotations varied by as much as 160 percent. Months of seeking quotations satisfied mitigation.

dorton.summary: An acceptance is “expressly conditional” under § 2-207(1) only if it clearly tells the offeror that the offeree will not proceed without assent to its additional terms; a form saying the sale was “subject to” its printed conditions did not qualify, so whether the arbitration clause entered the carpet contracts depended on § 2-207(2) and findings the district court had not made.

sections.Parties: Frank E. Dorton and his partners, doing business as The Carpet Mart in Kingsport, Tennessee, were the plaintiffs and appellees; they bought carpet for resale and claimed the seller misrepresented its fiber content. Collins & Aikman Corporation, a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in New York and a carpet plant in Dalton, Georgia, was the defendant and appellant seeking to enforce arbitration language in its printed sales forms. Both were merchants.
sections.Material Facts: From 1968 through 1970 the parties did more than fifty-five carpet transactions. Orders were telephoned to Collins & Aikman’s Georgia order department, sometimes by a Carpet Mart partner and sometimes through the seller’s visiting salesman; the parties disputed whether those calls themselves produced oral agreements. After checking price and credit the seller mailed a printed acknowledgment, in several versions, whose face said the transaction was subject to the terms on both sides and purported to bind the buyer by signing, giving shipping directions, accepting delivery, or in some versions keeping the form ten days without objection; the reverse required arbitration in New York City of disputes connected with the contract. The acknowledgment usually arrived before the carpet. The Carpet Mart accepted delivery and paid without objecting. In May 1970 a customer complaint led it to discover that carpet supposedly made entirely of Kodel polyester allegedly contained a cheaper, inferior fiber.
sections.Procedural History: The Carpet Mart sued in Tennessee state court for fraud, deceit and misrepresentation, seeking $450,000 in compensatory and punitive damages. Collins & Aikman removed the case on diversity grounds and moved under § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act to stay the litigation pending arbitration. The district court found no binding arbitration agreement: it applied § 2-207(3), treated the transactions as contracts formed by conduct, and excluded the seller’s unmatched arbitration clause. The seller appealed the denial of the stay, appealable under 28 U.S.C. § 1292. The Sixth Circuit, Judge Celebrezze writing, remanded on January 6, 1972 for findings on whether the oral dealings formed contracts, whether arbitration was already part of them, and if not whether it materially altered them; Judge Brooks participated but died before the opinion was filed.
sections.Issue: Did the seller’s acknowledgments make acceptance expressly conditional on the buyer’s assent to additional terms, so that the writings formed no contract and § 2-207(3) governed? If instead they were acceptances or confirmations under § 2-207(1), did the arbitration clause enter the contracts under subsection (2)? If it did, could the buyer’s fraud claims proceed in court without a stay?
sections.Holding: An acceptance is expressly conditional within § 2-207(1) only when it clearly conveys that the offeree will not proceed without the offeror’s assent to the additional or different terms. The seller’s “subject to” language and its provisions treating various acts or silence as acceptance did not meet that standard, so the district court could not bypass subsections (1) and (2) by applying subsection (3). If arbitration was additional to the oral offers or agreements, it had to be evaluated under subsection (2), where, between merchants, material alteration was the central question requiring factual findings; the court did not decide whether this clause was material. If the clause was part of the contracts, its breadth reached the fraud claims and required a stay. Remanded.
sections.Reasoning: Section 2-207 answers the commercial practice of exchanging forms whose boilerplate never matches. Under the mirror-image rule a response adding terms became a counteroffer; the Code lets a contract exist despite differing boilerplate and decides separately which added terms enter, so treating every qualified acknowledgment as a counteroffer would undo the statutory design. Two factual questions came first: whether the telephone dealings already completed contracts, making the acknowledgments confirmations rather than acceptances, and whether arbitration was in fact new. The conditional-acceptance proviso demanded more than a declaration that the seller’s terms governed: it required an express condition tied to the buyer’s assent, and a form offering several ways to bind the buyer did not distinctly say the seller would refuse to proceed without assurance of assent. Once the acknowledgments were acceptances or confirmations, subsection (2) governed the added clause; the court left materiality to the trial court. Finally, under Prima Paint a broad arbitration clause, if agreed, covers a claim that the sale was induced by fraud, because the buyer attacked the carpet rather than the procurement of the clause itself.

citoh.summary: A seller’s acknowledgment that expressly conditioned acceptance on the buyer’s assent to its additional terms formed no contract through the writings, but delivery and payment formed one under § 2-207(3) whose terms were those on which the writings agreed plus the Code’s gap-fillers; the seller’s unagreed arbitration clause was neither, so it dropped out.

sections.Parties: C. Itoh & Co. (America) Inc., the steel buyer, was the plaintiff and appellee, suing for allegedly defective steel and late delivery. The Jordan International Company, the seller, was the defendant and appellant, contending that the dispute had to be arbitrated under its acknowledgment form and seeking a stay pending arbitration. Judge Sprecher wrote for the Seventh Circuit on April 4, 1977.
sections.Material Facts: Itoh sent Jordan a purchase order for steel coils. Jordan responded with an acknowledgment form whose language expressly conditioned the seller’s acceptance on the buyer’s assent to the additional or different terms on its face and reverse, and directed the buyer to notify the seller at once if the terms were unacceptable. One reverse-side provision required arbitration; Itoh’s purchase order contained no arbitration clause and Itoh never assented to the added terms. The writings therefore did not agree on arbitration. Jordan nevertheless delivered the steel and Itoh paid for it. Itoh later complained that the steel was defective and had arrived late; the dispute surfaced after Itoh’s own customer, Riverview Steel, alleged defects and refused payment.
sections.Procedural History: Itoh sued Jordan for the alleged defects and late delivery. Jordan moved to stay the proceedings pending arbitration under its acknowledgment, and the district court denied the motion on a judicial-economy ground. Jordan appealed. The Seventh Circuit rejected the district court’s rationale, because the Federal Arbitration Act requires a stay whenever an arbitration agreement exists, but affirmed the denial because no agreement to arbitrate had ever been formed. This account follows the casebook’s excerpt of the opinion (Farnsworth, seventh edition, pp. 199–201); the brief did not independently verify the full reported text.
sections.Issue: When a seller expressly conditions acceptance on the buyer’s assent to additional terms, the buyer does not assent, and both parties nevertheless perform, does § 2-207(3) create a contract? If so, can the seller’s arbitration clause become one of its terms through the buyer’s receipt and payment or through the provision for supplementary Code terms?
sections.Holding: Jordan’s acknowledgment satisfied the expressly-conditional proviso of § 2-207(1), so the exchange of writings formed no contract and the acknowledgment operated as a counteroffer. The parties’ performance nevertheless established a contract under § 2-207(3), whose terms were those on which the writings agreed together with supplementary terms incorporated under the Code. The writings did not agree on arbitration and Article 2 supplies no arbitration term as a gap-filler, so the clause was excluded; delivery and payment proved the sale without proving assent to the added clause. The denial of the stay was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Jordan’s form used the condition Dorton’s forms lacked: it tied acceptance expressly to the buyer’s assent to additional or different terms, which prevented formation through the writings unless that condition was met. The failure of the writings did not end the matter, because § 2-207(3) recognizes contracts demonstrated by both parties’ conduct: Jordan delivered and Itoh paid, objective evidence of a sale the Code would not treat as nonexistent merely because the forms failed to match. The same subsection fixed the terms. Its agreed-terms rule excluded the arbitration clause because the buyer’s order never agreed to it. Nor could the clause return as a supplementary term, since that phrase refers to Article 2’s standardized gap-fillers, which complete a contract with default obligations rather than importing disputed boilerplate the agreed-terms rule has just excluded. A seller that chooses an expressly conditional form gains freedom from commitment through the writings and can withhold delivery until it obtains assent; if it delivers without assent, it accepts the risk that the conduct-based contract will omit its unagreed terms.

lefkowitz.summary: A newspaper advertisement that names the item, the price, the time and the first person entitled to buy is a definite offer accepted by appearing first and tendering the price; the advertiser cannot then impose a house rule, such as “women only,” that the advertisement never stated.

sections.Parties: Morris Lefkowitz, the customer and plaintiff, was the respondent on appeal and represented himself. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store, Inc., the merchant and defendant, appealed an order refusing to amend the trial court’s findings or grant a new trial. Justice Murphy wrote for the Supreme Court of Minnesota on December 20, 1957.
sections.Material Facts: The store ran two advertisements a week apart. On April 6, 1956 it advertised three new fur coats “worth to $100” for one dollar each, available at 9 a.m. the following Saturday, first come first served. On April 13 it advertised two pastel mink three-skin scarfs described as selling for $89.50 and one black lapin stole “worth $139.50” for one dollar each, again at 9 a.m. Saturday, first come first served. On each Saturday Lefkowitz arrived first at the counter, demanded the advertised item and said he was ready to pay one dollar. The store refused both times: on the first visit it invoked an internal house rule limiting the offer to women, and on the second it relied on his knowledge of that rule from the previous week. Neither advertisement mentioned the restriction.
sections.Procedural History: Lefkowitz sued for breach of contract in the Municipal Court of Minneapolis. The court denied recovery for the coats because the only evidence of their value was the indefinite “worth to $100,” but accepted the stole’s stated value of $139.50 and awarded that sum less the one-dollar price, $138.50. The store moved for amended findings or a new trial; the municipal court denied the motion, and the store appealed that denial. The Supreme Court of Minnesota affirmed, leaving the $138.50 award in place. There was no dissent.
sections.Issue: Did the advertisement commit the store to sell on the stated terms once a customer performed the requested acts, or merely invite customers to make offers the store could refuse? Did Lefkowitz’s arrival and offer to pay accept it, and could the store enforce its unstated women-only rule afterward?
sections.Holding: Ordinary advertisements often invite offers, but an advertisement that is clear, definite and explicit and leaves nothing open for negotiation is an offer, and performance of its terms forms a contract. The stole advertisement identified the article, an exact price, the time and the eligible purchaser by order of arrival, so it was an offer; Lefkowitz accepted by arriving first and offering the price. Having accepted, he could not be met with new or arbitrary conditions absent from the published offer, and his prior knowledge of the house rule did not write it into the second advertisement. The award of $138.50 was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: The legal character of an advertisement depends on its language and circumstances. Here the terms supplied both the store’s obligation and the person entitled to enforce it: one stole, one dollar, 9 a.m. Saturday, first come first served. Those terms also answered the usual objection to treating advertisements as offers, that a merchant might be bound beyond its stock, because the quantity and the taker were fixed. Lefkowitz accepted by doing exactly what the offer requested. An advertiser may modify or withdraw an offer before acceptance, but it cannot impose new or arbitrary conditions afterward, and the women-only rule was such a condition because the advertisement never stated it. The court resolved the case on the terms and timing of formation and did not treat it as a sex-discrimination claim. It also separated liability from proof of loss: the coats’ stated maximum of $100 did not establish what any coat was worth, so that claim failed for uncertain valuation, while the stole’s definite stated value supported an award of the value less the price.

wucherpfennig.summary: A response that announces readiness to proceed and financing arranged but asks the offeror what exact amount she expects, and whether she will sign a special-use-valuation agreement, is not the absolute and unequivocal acceptance North Dakota requires; it continued negotiations, so the offeror was free to revoke.

sections.Parties: Donald Wucherpfennig, the plaintiff and appellant, sought specific performance of an alleged contract to buy his sister’s interest in inherited farmland. Elizabeth Dooley, his sister, was the defendant and appellee. Their sister Louise Grettum and others claiming interests in the land were also named, though the disputed sale concerned only Elizabeth’s share. Justice Sand wrote for the Supreme Court of North Dakota on July 11, 1984.
sections.Material Facts: The siblings inherited a farm of four quarters after their father died in 1964 and their mother in 1977: Donald held an undivided two-thirds of the farmstead quarter and each sister one-sixth, and each held one-third of the other three quarters. During probate Elizabeth wrote on January 4, 1979 to Robert Case, the estate’s attorney, offering to sell her share to Donald at $200 an acre for cash, handled promptly; no one disputed that this was an offer. Case replied on January 13 that Donald was interested. On February 17 Case wrote that Donald had arranged Federal Land Bank financing and was ready to proceed, then asked Elizabeth to state the exact amount she expected for her interest and whether she would sign a Special Use Valuation agreement, requesting a response on both. She did not answer, and on March 9 she revoked the offer.
sections.Procedural History: Donald sued for specific performance of the alleged sale and, alternatively, for partition. By consent the specific-performance claim was tried first. The district court found that Donald had not accepted Elizabeth’s offer and that even if he had, the supposed contract could not be specifically enforced, giving four independently sufficient grounds for dismissal. On appeal Donald had to defeat every ground. The Supreme Court of North Dakota agreed that there was no acceptance, expressly declined to decide the other issues, and affirmed the dismissal; the partition claim was not resolved in the reported decision.
sections.Issue: Did the February 17 letter, stating that Donald had arranged financing and was ready to proceed while asking Elizabeth for the exact amount she expected and about a special-use-valuation agreement, communicate an unconditional acceptance that formed a contract before she revoked on March 9?
sections.Holding: No. Under N.D. Century Code § 9-03-21 and the governing precedents, an acceptance must be absolute, unequivocal and unconditional, must concern the same bargain as the offer, and must express an intention to create the contract through that response itself. Read as a whole, the letter showed preparation and continued interest but left a material aspect of the exchange open and contemplated further negotiation; Donald had not unequivocally committed himself to the transaction Elizabeth described. The dismissal of the specific-performance claim was affirmed on that ground alone.
sections.Reasoning: The court read the letter as a whole. Arranging financing showed Donald was preparing to buy and readiness to proceed showed continuing interest, but the immediate request for the amount Elizabeth expected indicated that a material part of the exchange remained open, so the letter was movement toward a future agreement rather than assent that itself completed the bargain. Donald’s own testimony reinforced the reading: asked why the letter named no total, he said the amount would have been $37,200, acknowledged that Elizabeth would have expected more, and admitted she would not have signed a contract stating his figure. The parties therefore had not assented to the same terms. Under Restatement §§ 59 and 61 a reply conditioning assent on different terms is a counteroffer, while a completed acceptance may carry a nonconditional request; here the threshold commitment was missing, so the court did not need to classify the letter as a counteroffer. Donald’s financing arrangements showed preparation, not acceptance of a cash-sale offer, and reliance was not treated as a formation argument.

international-filter.summary: The buyer’s signed order, which by its terms became a contract when approved by an executive officer at the seller’s Chicago office, was the offer, and the executive’s dated “O.K.” was the prescribed acceptance; because the offer designated that act as sufficient, no separate notice of approval was required, and the seller’s acknowledgment letter would have sufficed as notice in any event.

sections.Parties: International Filter Company, an Illinois manufacturer of water-purification equipment with its principal office in Chicago, was the plaintiff and the party seeking review. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Company, a Texas company making ice in Conroe, was the defendant. Judge Nickels wrote for Section A of the Texas Commission of Appeals on December 10, 1925, and Chief Justice Cureton adopted the recommended disposition for the Texas Supreme Court.
sections.Material Facts: On February 10, 1920 International Filter’s traveling representative, W. W. Waterman, presented Conroe’s manager, Henry Thompson, with a written proposal for a No. 2 Junior steel-tank water softener and filter at $1,230, f.o.b. Chicago. The form provided that the proposal became a contract when accepted by the purchaser and approved by an executive officer of International Filter at its Chicago office, and that it was submitted for prompt acceptance. Thompson signed an acceptance that day and asked for shipment by March 10. On February 13 P. N. Engel, the company’s president, wrote a dated approval on the paper; on February 14 the company mailed a letter thanking Conroe for the order, confirming the March 10 shipment and asking for a water sample. Conroe received the letter, then tried to cancel on February 28 and again on March 4; International Filter denied any right to cancel on March 2.
sections.Procedural History: International Filter sued for breach. After a trial without a jury the court entered judgment for Conroe on the formation issues and other material issues, and the Court of Civil Appeals affirmed, 269 S.W. 210, agreeing that Engel’s endorsement was an approval within the form but treating the absence of notice as the obstacle. On further review the Commission of Appeals recommended reversal and remand to the intermediate court for questions properly presented but not yet decided, and the Texas Supreme Court adopted that disposition. A favorable ruling on formation therefore did not end the breach action or produce a damages award.
sections.Issue: Who made the legally operative offer, what act accepted it, and did International Filter have to notify Conroe of the executive approval before Conroe lost its power to withdraw? Alternatively, did the February 14 acknowledgment letter communicate approval if notice was required?
sections.Holding: Conroe’s signed order was the offer, even though International Filter drafted the form and called it a proposal, because the form reserved a further act of approval for the seller’s executive officer. Engel’s dated endorsement was approval by an executive officer at the designated place and completed the contract. The writing made that act sufficient and required no separate notice, so the claimed oral demand for prompt notification did not change the written terms. In any event the February 14 letter, read by a reasonable recipient, communicated the approval. The judgment was reversed and the case remanded to the Court of Civil Appeals.
sections.Reasoning: Drafting the form and making the offer are separate roles: because the paper reserved approval by International Filter’s executive, Conroe’s signature supplied the offer. Engel’s dated endorsement was that act. Notice ordinarily protects an offeror who seeks a return promise, but the offeror may dispense with it by authorizing a particular act as sufficient acceptance; drawing on Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co., the court held that an offeree completes acceptance by following the method the offer makes sufficient. The writing said the proposal became a contract upon the executive’s approval in Chicago, and requiring notice to arrive in Conroe would add a condition and change both the time and place of formation; the prompt-acceptance clause governed when approval had to occur, not an additional form of acceptance. Alternatively, a notice may communicate acceptance by reasonable implication: the letter thanked the buyer for the specified order, confirmed the shipment and requested the water sample, so a reasonable recipient would understand it to convey approval. Unlike White v. Corlies & Tifft, the offeree here performed an observable act the offer itself made sufficient.

white-corlies.summary: An offer made to a party at a distance is accepted only by an outward act placed in a proper course of communication so that it will ordinarily reach the offeror; a builder’s private decision to accept, followed by buying and working lumber equally suited to other jobs, communicated nothing and was mere preparation, so the merchants could still countermand.

sections.Parties: White, a builder with a business on Fortieth Street in New York City, was the plaintiff and respondent on appeal. Corlies and Tifft, merchants doing business on Dey Street who wanted a suite of offices at 57 Broadway fitted up, were the defendants and appellants. Judge Folger wrote for the Court of Appeals of New York on November 20, 1871; the casebook spells the name Tift.
sections.Material Facts: In September 1865 the merchants gave White specifications for fitting up the offices and asked for an estimate, which he delivered on September 28; they changed the specifications that day and he assented to the changes, but no agreement was complete. They had first wanted black walnut within twenty-one days, which White said he could not do, then asked for an estimate in white pine; his estimate named no completion time. On September 29 their bookkeeper sent White a note saying that upon an agreement to finish the fitting up of the offices within two weeks from that date he could begin at once. White did not reply. He at once bought lumber and began working on it at his own shop; the lumber and the work suited other comparable jobs. The next day the merchants countermanded the proposal and asked for another estimate in black walnut.
sections.Procedural History: White sued for damages, contending that his conduct had accepted the proposal before the countermand. The trial judge instructed the jury that White need not have gone back to the merchants and said he had begun, and that he could act on the note and commence the job; the defendants excepted. The jury found for White, and the General Term of the First Judicial District affirmed. The Court of Appeals reversed and ordered a new trial, with costs to abide the event; Justice Allen did not vote.
sections.Issue: Did White accept the merchants’ September 29 proposal by privately deciding to proceed and by buying and working on materials suitable for any comparable job, without any act that communicated assent to the merchants or set such a communication in motion?
sections.Holding: No. The note was a proposal requiring acceptance, and an offer made when the parties are apart must be accepted by an appropriate outward act. The act need not have reached the offeror’s knowledge before a contract forms, but it must be put in a proper course of communication so that it will ordinarily reach the offeror within a reasonable time. White’s private intention, and his purchase of lumber usable on other jobs, gave the merchants no indication of assent and did not set one in motion; they were preparation, not acceptance. The instruction was erroneous and a new trial was ordered.
sections.Reasoning: The court found no earlier contract in the evidence and treated the bookkeeper’s note as a proposal requiring acceptance. Where parties are apart, assent must be shown by an outward act: a mailed acceptance illustrates the distinction, because dispatch may complete the contract before delivery when the offeree has taken an objectively communicative step. White’s conduct failed that test. The lumber he bought and the work he did on it suited other jobs of the kind, so his acts did not identify this undertaking as the one accepted; his private intention explained them to himself but gave the merchants no outward sign. The court did not hold that conduct can never accept an offer or that actual receipt of notice is always required, only that general preparations coupled with an uncommunicated intention were insufficient under this proposal. Under the later Restatement the case would be analysed by asking whether the offer invited a promise or performance and by separating preparation from the beginning of invited performance under §§ 45 and 62, with §§ 54 and 56 addressing notice.

ricketts.summary: A grandfather’s gratuitous $2,000 note, given so that his granddaughter would no longer have to work, was enforceable against his estate: although her quitting was not the bargained-for price of the note, he intentionally induced her to change her position in reliance on it, so equitable estoppel barred the executor from pleading want of consideration.

sections.Parties: Katie Scothorn, John C. Ricketts’s granddaughter and a bookkeeper who left her job after receiving his note, was the plaintiff and defendant in error; she obtained judgment on the note. Andrew D. Ricketts, executor of John C. Ricketts’s estate, was the defendant and plaintiff in error, resisting enforcement for want of consideration. Justice Sullivan wrote for the Supreme Court of Nebraska on December 8, 1898.
sections.Material Facts: On May 1, 1891 John C. Ricketts signed a note promising to pay Katie Scothorn $2,000 on demand with six percent annual interest. She was then a bookkeeper for Mayer Brothers earning $10 a week. Around nine that morning he visited her at the store, took the note from his vest, and told her he had fixed things so she would not have to work any more, adding that none of his other grandchildren worked and she need not either. She took the note, kissed him, cried, and soon gave up the position. She stayed out of work for more than a year; in September 1892, with his consent, she took a bookkeeping job with Funke & Ogden. He paid one year’s interest, said he would pay the note when he sold his Ohio farm, and never repudiated it. He died on June 8, 1894.
sections.Procedural History: Scothorn sued the executor on the note in the District Court of Lancaster County, alleging that Ricketts gave it to induce her to give up her job and that she relied on it for support. The executor denied the allegations and pleaded want of consideration. The material facts were undisputed at trial and Scothorn recovered judgment. The executor brought error to the Nebraska Supreme Court, challenging the note’s admission, the sufficiency of consideration and the treatment of the undisputed evidence. The court held that equitable estoppel barred the defense as a matter of law, treated any trial error as harmless because only one result was possible, and affirmed.
sections.Issue: When a grandfather gives his working granddaughter a gratuitous promissory note while reasonably contemplating that she will leave her job, and she does leave in reliance on the note, may his executor assert lack of consideration to defeat enforcement?
sections.Holding: No. The note was a promised gift: Ricketts requested no return performance and Scothorn made no bargained-for promise, so ordinary consideration was lacking. But he intentionally influenced her to alter her position for the worse on the faith of the note, in a way he could reasonably foresee, and equitable estoppel therefore precluded his executor from asserting want of consideration. The judgment enforcing the note was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Consideration requires a performance or return promise sought in exchange for the promisor’s commitment. Ricketts imposed no condition and asked for nothing; he meant to give his granddaughter financial independence, leaving her free to work or not, so her resignation was a consequence of the gift promise rather than its price. The court then turned to the charitable-subscription cases; those opinions often called the induced expenditure consideration, but the real principle at work was equitable estoppel. Estoppel in pais arises from conduct that induces another to change position in accordance with the actor’s real or apparent intention, and it precludes the actor from later asserting a right against the person who relied in good faith and changed position for the worse. Ricketts tied the note directly to Scothorn’s freedom from work; her resignation was a reasonable and probable response to his words and the promised income; she gave up a $10-a-week position. Her later return to work did not undo reliance that had already occurred. The case predates § 90 and reaches, through estoppel language, what later writers called promissory estoppel.

feinberg.summary: A board resolution promising a long-serving employee $200 a month for life whenever she chose to retire lacked consideration, because past service cannot be bargained for and she promised no further work, but her retirement from a well-paid job in reliance on it made the promise binding under Restatement § 90; the induced act was the 1949 retirement, not her later illness.

sections.Parties: Anna Sacks Feinberg, a former Pfeiffer employee who retired in reliance on the company’s promise of $200 a month for life, was the plaintiff and respondent. Pfeiffer Company, formerly S. Pfeiffer Manufacturing Company, a pharmaceutical maker whose board adopted the pension resolution and whose later management cut the payments, was the defendant and appellant. Commissioner Doerner wrote the opinion, which the St. Louis Court of Appeals adopted per curiam on March 17, 1959.
sections.Material Facts: Feinberg began working for Pfeiffer in 1910 at seventeen and by 1947 was bookkeeper, office manager and assistant treasurer. On December 27, 1947 the board, recognized her long, faithful service, raised her salary from $350 to $400 a month, and resolved that she could retire whenever she chose and receive $200 a month for life, while hoping she would keep working for many years. Her employment remained at will and she promised no future service, testifying she would have kept working without the resolution. She retired on June 30, 1949 at fifty-seven, healthy, after she and her husband calculated that his earnings plus the pension would support them. Pfeiffer paid $200 monthly until new management, advised that no obligation existed, sent a $100 check on April 1, 1956; she refused it and sued. At trial she was sixty-five and, after cancer surgery in November 1957, unable to work.
sections.Procedural History: Feinberg sued in the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis on the promise of $200 a month for life. The parties waived a jury, and the court entered judgment for $5,100 in accrued installments through trial plus interest. Pfeiffer appealed, challenging evidentiary rulings, the findings on reliance and the legal sufficiency of the promise. Missouri statutes required the appellate court to review the law and the evidence and enter the judgment the trial court should have entered; it affirmed, and rehearing and transfer to the Missouri Supreme Court were denied. The casebook prints the consideration discussion and the reliance discussion as two excerpts of this one opinion.
sections.Issue: Was the pension promise supported by consideration in Feinberg’s past service or her continued employment? If not, did her retirement in reliance on the promise make it binding under promissory estoppel, notwithstanding the company’s argument that her later disability, not the promise, explained her inability to work?
sections.Holding: Past service was not consideration, because acts already performed cannot be sought in exchange for a later promise, and continued employment was not, because the resolution let her retire immediately and she promised no further work. Retirement, however, was action the company should reasonably have expected its resolution to induce, and the promise did induce it: she gave up a lucrative position while still able to work. Under § 90 of the First Restatement the promise was binding because injustice could be avoided only by enforcement. The $5,100 judgment plus interest was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Pfeiffer adopted the pension after thirty-seven years of service; those completed acts had been rendered under the existing employment and could not have been the price of a promise made in 1947. Nor did the following eighteen months of work: the resolution allowed immediate retirement and attached no service condition. Retirement was different. Section 90 of the First Restatement binds a promise the promisor should reasonably expect to induce definite and substantial action or forbearance that it does induce, when only enforcement can avoid injustice. The board deliberately created a retirement privilege exercisable whenever Feinberg chose, so retirement was the very conduct the promise invited; the trial judge credited her testimony that she could have kept working and planned her household around the pension. Injustice followed from the surrender of a well-paid position at fifty-seven and nearly seven years of payments before the company tried to halve them, by which time comparable employment was realistically unavailable. Her 1957 cancer strengthened the consequences but did not control enforceability, since the induced act was the 1949 retirement. The court treated Ricketts v. Scothorn as closely analogous.

cohen-cowles.summary: The First Amendment does not bar applying Minnesota’s generally applicable promissory-estoppel law to newspapers that broke reporters’ promises of confidentiality and named a political source; on remand Minnesota found a clear promise, intended inducement, reliance and injustice, and reinstated the $200,000 verdict.

sections.Parties: Dan Cohen, an experienced political and public-relations operative working with Wheelock Whitney’s Independent-Republican campaign for governor, was the plaintiff and the petitioner in the Supreme Court. Cowles Media Company, publisher of the Minneapolis Star and Tribune, and Northwest Publications, Inc., publisher of the St. Paul Pioneer Press Dispatch, were the defendants and respondents. Reporters Lori Sturdevant and Bill Salisbury promised anonymity and objected when editors overruled them. The records concerned Marlene Johnson, the Democratic-Farmer-Labor candidate for lieutenant governor.
sections.Material Facts: On October 27, 1982, days before Minnesota’s gubernatorial election, Cohen separately offered Sturdevant and Salisbury documents about a candidate on condition that his identity stay anonymous and they not investigate his source; each reporter agreed, intending to keep the promise. The documents were public court records showing that Johnson had been charged in 1969 with unlawful assembly (dismissed) and convicted in 1970 of petit theft (later vacated); Johnson explained the first as a protest over minority hiring and the second as leaving a store with six dollars of sewing materials while distraught over her father’s death. Editors at both papers judged the partisan source part of the story and expected competitors to identify Cohen; the reporters objected strongly and Sturdevant withheld her byline. On October 28 both papers named Cohen and his campaign connection, the Star Tribune also naming his advertising employer, which fired him that day.
sections.Procedural History: Cohen sued both publishers in Minnesota state court for breach of contract and fraudulent misrepresentation; the jury awarded $200,000 in compensatory damages and $250,000 in punitive damages against each paper on the fraud claim. The Court of Appeals, 2–1, vacated the punitive awards because the reporters had intended to keep their promises and affirmed contract liability, 445 N.W.2d 248 (1989). The Minnesota Supreme Court reversed on contract, treating source confidentiality as an ethical rather than legal commitment, then raised promissory estoppel itself and held that enforcing the promise would offend the First Amendment, 457 N.W.2d 199 (1990). The United States Supreme Court reversed 5–4, Justice White writing, 501 U.S. 663 (1991). On remand the Minnesota Supreme Court, Justice Simonett writing, found promissory estoppel established on the existing record and reinstated the $200,000 judgment, 479 N.W.2d 387 (1992).
sections.Issue: Does the First Amendment bar recovery under a state’s generally applicable promissory-estoppel law when newspapers break promises of source confidentiality and publish truthful information? On remand, did the record establish promissory estoppel under Minnesota law, and could the existing $200,000 verdict be reinstated?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court held that the First Amendment permits applying Minnesota’s generally applicable promissory-estoppel doctrine to the press: judicial enforcement is state action, but the doctrine governs promises in everyday transactions and imposes no burden peculiar to the press, so the newspapers had to bear the legal consequences of promises they chose to make. It reversed and remanded without reinstating damages. The Minnesota Supreme Court then held that the reporters gave a clear promise designed to induce disclosure, that Cohen relied by delivering the records, that publication cost him his job, and that injustice required a remedy; it declined broader protection under the state press clause, found no public policy against enforcement, and reinstated the $200,000 compensatory judgment.
sections.Reasoning: Justice White placed promissory estoppel with the labor, antitrust, tax and copyright laws that bind the press on the same terms as everyone else; the newspapers had obtained Cohen’s identity together with a promise restricting its use, so any resulting damages were a cost of how the information was acquired. The truthful-publication cases requiring an interest of the highest order did not apply, because liability arose from a self-imposed promise rather than a state penalty on publication, and Cohen sought economic losses from breach rather than redress for hurtful statements. On remand Minnesota excused Cohen’s failure to plead promissory estoppel because enforceability of the promise had driven the case from the start and both sides had briefed it; it found the promise unambiguous and made to obtain the documents, Cohen’s reliance and firing established, and injustice, a legal question, shown by newsroom custom, the reporters’ own objections and the absence of a compelling need to name him. Neither the state press clause nor public policy barred enforcement, and the jury’s foreseeability instruction fit reliance relief, so the $200,000 verdict stood without retrial.

cohen-cowles.separateOpinions: Justice Blackmun, joined by Justices Marshall and Souter, dissented: the case fit the truthful-publication line, so Minnesota needed an interest of the highest order, which compensating a source for a broken promise was not. Justice Souter, joined by Marshall, Blackmun and O’Connor, favored case-specific balancing and thought voters’ interest in learning an election-eve leaker’s identity outweighed the state’s interest in enforcing the promise.

dg-stout.summary: A supplier’s assurance that it would keep an at-will distributorship cannot support recovery of future profits, but it can support reliance damages for a priced sale opportunity the distributor gave up on the strength of the assurance; the Seventh Circuit sent the case to trial, where the distributor recovered $394,050 plus interest.

sections.Parties: D & G Stout, Inc., successor to General Liquors, Inc., the operating distributor the opinions call General, was the plaintiff and appellant. Bacardi Imports, Inc., a major liquor supplier that used General as its northern Indiana wholesale distributor, was the defendant and appellee. National Wine & Spirits Company, a competing distributor, offered to buy General’s assets; Hiram Walker, another supplier, later withdrew its line.
sections.Material Facts: General, based in South Bend, had distributed Bacardi products in northern Indiana at will for more than thirty-five years. In spring 1987 two major suppliers withdrew their lines, and General’s president, David Stout, concluded it could stay profitable if it kept Bacardi, Hiram Walker and Canandaigua. On July 9 National’s James LaCrosse approached Stout about buying General, and at a Bacardi meeting in Indianapolis that day Stout disclosed the contemplated sale and sought a commitment; Bacardi emphatically said it intended to stay. General and National negotiated an asset sale over two weeks. By July 22–23 the financial terms were settled; Stout again sought assurances, Bacardi unequivocally recommitted, and General rejected National’s offer on July 23. That afternoon Bacardi decided to move its line and told General on July 30. General sold to National on August 28 at a price it said was $550,000 below the July proposal.
sections.Procedural History: D & G Stout sued Bacardi in the Northern District of Indiana under diversity jurisdiction for the decline in the business’s sale value on a promissory-estoppel theory. Judge Robert L. Miller, Jr. granted Bacardi summary judgment, treating an open-ended at-will assurance as one Indiana law would not let General rely on. The Seventh Circuit (Cudahy, J., with Posner and Flaum, JJ.) reversed on January 31, 1991, 923 F.2d 566, and remanded for trial. After a bench trial the district court found the promise conditional on market and performance conditions and Bacardi unaware of the National negotiations, but found every element of promissory estoppel under an objective foreseeability standard and awarded $394,050 in reliance damages plus $116,400 in prejudgment interest, 805 F. Supp. 1434 (1992).
sections.Issue: At summary judgment, did Indiana promissory-estoppel law permit General to seek the value of a known sale opportunity it allegedly surrendered in reasonable reliance on Bacardi’s assurance of a continuing at-will distributorship, or did the at-will nature of the relationship make such reliance unreasonable and the claimed loss an impermissible demand for future profits?
sections.Holding: The claim could proceed. Because the assurance fixed no term, General could not recover expected future profits from Bacardi sales, but it could recover reliance damages for the existing National opportunity it allegedly gave up. Bacardi knew General was deciding whether to sell, repeatedly encouraged it to continue, and could foresee an immediate loss of bargaining position if it withdrew. Summary judgment was reversed and the case remanded for proof of the promise, reliance, causation and damages.
sections.Reasoning: Indiana’s § 90 rule binds a promise that foreseeably induces action or forbearance when enforcement is needed to avoid injustice, with relief calibrated to justice. The court drew an analogy to an indefinite at-will job offer: it supplies no fixed future wage because discharge can follow hiring immediately, yet Indiana cases protect reliance costs such as moving expenses and wages forgone in preparing for the job. General sought the value of a priced July sale it surrendered by choosing to continue, and Bacardi’s withdrawal then destroyed that alternative and General’s leverage. National already carried a competing rum and never expected to keep the Bacardi account, so the price drop measured the loss of General’s independent-operation alternative rather than the capitalized value of Bacardi profits. The later trial refined the picture: the promise was conditional and Bacardi lacked actual knowledge of the National talks, but it knew its line was essential to General’s survival and should have expected General to forgo exit opportunities; comparing the rejected July terms with the August recoveries, the court awarded $510,450 in all.
